transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-23
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 55m
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood CSM); Marcus Chen (CTO, Atlas Finance), Leah Ortiz (Lead ML Engineer), Daniel Park (DevOps), Rita Alvarez (Security)

Summary:
Quick sync to walk through Redwood's autoscaling and capacity planning for Atlas' plan to move inference for risk-scoring models into production. Focus on burst policies, queueing models, reserved GPUs, KV cache behavior across scaled replicas, and VPC/on-prem constraints.

Topics:
- Autoscaling triggers (latency SLO vs CPU/GPU utilization)
- Queueing/backpressure and request shaping
- Reserved GPU pools and burst capacity
- KV cache sharding / warming and cold-start impact
- Batching/quantization tradeoffs for p99/p95 latency
- VPC peering, egress, and private deployment considerations

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Marcus, Leah, Daniel, Rita — and from our side Priya and Samir. Quick agenda, go over your traffic profile, then dive into autoscale and capacity planning, and end with next steps.
[00:14] Marcus Chen: Yeah thanks Jordan, short context: we run a risk-scoring pipeline that calls two models — a short completion for triage and a longer contextual scoring model. Right now on-prem with spot instances, want to move to a more predictable infra; interested in Redwood Dedicated or Private.
[00:30] Leah Ortiz: Our p95 target for the short model is 120ms and for the scoring model p95 is 600ms, p99 around 1.2s. Peak concurrency right now is about 450 concurrent requests, RPS spikes to 800 for 2-3 mins during market open.
[00:48] Priya Raman: Okay those are super helpful. Quick clarifying q: when you say concurrent do you mean in-flight tokens (open streams) or request-level concurrency?
[00:55] Leah Ortiz: Request-level mostly, we do streaming so some requests keep sockets open.
[01:04] Priya Raman: Got it, streaming opens the need to account for long-lived connections in autoscaling. Two approaches we typically use: SLO-driven autoscale (target p95 latency at route level) and utilization-based (GPU occupancy). We'll go through tradeoffs.
[01:19] Daniel Park: Also network constraints — our security team requires fixed egress IPs for the managed control plane to talk to our VPC, otherwise the firewall blocks. That affects burst capacity if peering takes time.
[01:31] Rita Alvarez: And SOC2/ISO questions: we need audit logs for autoscale events and scaling triggers for compliance — who can see scaling decisions.
[01:40] Jordan Lee: Yep, we have audit logs and role-level events exposed in the Console. We'll share the runbook with event samples.

[05:02] Priya Raman: Let me paint the common queueing model we recommend: an in-memory per-node request queue with admission control. We cap queue depth to limit tail latency — if queue is full we either shed or route to fallback model. For reserved GPU pools we provision steady-state replicas and allow short-lived burst instances that can start in ~30-90s depending on region and instance family.
[05:30] Leah Ortiz: 30-90s startup for GPUs is big — during our 2-3 minute spikes that's sometimes too slow. Can we do faster bursts?
[05:40] Priya Raman: Two levers — keep a small warm pool of standby reserved GPUs with pre-warmed model kernels and KV cache warmed (this is a low-cost reserved buffer), or use very short-lived micro-burst VMs for routing but accept cold KV cache impact. Warm buffer reduces cold-start tokens but costs more.
[05:58] Marcus Chen: How big should the warm pool be? Percent of peak?
[06:05] Priya Raman: We usually recommend 10-20% of peak concurrent capacity as a warm buffer for bursty workloads with short spikes. For your 800 RPS spikes, something like reserving capacity for 80–160 concurrent inference lanes. But we will do a capacity planning exercise against your traffic histogram.

[09:10] Priya Raman: About KV cache: it's per-replica — if you scale horizontally the KV caches are not shared, so there's a cache miss penalty when requests land on replicas that haven't seen that prefix. That means autoscaling strategies that churn replicas cause higher token cost and latency until caches warm. We mitigate with sticky routing or cache-warming pre-scripts.
[09:35] Daniel Park: Sticky routing sounds promising but does it break load balance?
[09:39] Priya Raman: We do hybrid: short sticky routing by user-id for a short TTL so hot users stick to a warmed replica, but we still rebalance over longer windows. Also you can provide a cache-warm list during scale-up — Redwood can prefetch KV entries from a provided keyset.
[10:00] Leah Ortiz: Prefetching KV — is there an API?
[10:03] Priya Raman: Yes, we'll share the endpoint in the runbook (see shared doc link). Typically you pass a list of hot prefixes and we schedule pre-warm on new replicas.

[12:22] Marcus Chen: On batching and quantization — our scoring model is 7B and can be quantized; we care about p99. If we enable larger batch sizes to improve throughput, p99 latency might degrade. What's the tradeoff?
[12:36] Priya Raman: Exactly. Two knobs: dynamic batching with SLO-aware thresholds (we will only batch up to X ms to avoid adding tail latencies), and model quantization profiles for steady-state cost reduction. For p99 you'll probably want conservative max batch sizes and an aggressive latency cap for batching. Quantization (8-bit/4-bit) reduces GPU memory and may improve throughput, but can add some quality degradation — our Optimize tooling suggests quant profiles per workload.
[13:05] Jordan Lee: Also note you can create separate routes: a low-latency route (no batching, higher cost) and a high-throughput route (batching+quant) and route traffic by traffic class or percentage.

[16:40] Priya Raman: On autoscale triggers — we support: 1) request-based (RPS with smoothing window), 2) latency-based (p95/p99), 3) GPU utilization (occupancy), and 4) custom signals (external orchestrator). For Atlas, given streaming and long-lived connections, we suggested p95 as primary with GPU occupancy as a secondary safeguard.
[16:59] Daniel Park: What smoothing windows do you use to avoid oscillation?
[17:04] Priya Raman: Typically 30s–120s smoothing with cooldown periods. For burstiness we add a short-term fast path: if RPS spike crosses a threshold, bring up warm buffer instances immediately and reroute best-effort traffic. Then if spike persists, scale more replicas.

[20:12] Leah Ortiz: For reserved GPUs — if we commit to a Dedicated pool, do we get guaranteed lower startup times?
[20:20] Priya Raman: Yes, Dedicated pools have pre-allocated instances so you can get <30s warm starts for additional replicas since the underlying VMs are already reserved; the remaining time is mostly kernel initialization and KV warm. If you go Private on-prem, startup may be similar but depends on your infra.
[20:36] Marcus Chen: How do we model cost vs latency for different configs?
[20:40] Jordan Lee: We'll run a cost/latency sensitivity analysis — sample outputs: cost per 1M tokens across configs, p95 delta. We'll include recommendations: reserved buffer size, quantization profile, batching cap. We'll share a spreadsheet after we get your trace.

[25:05] Priya Raman: Another practical point — shedding and graceful degradation. If queues fill we can reroute to a lightweight heuristic model or a cached response for stale but safe defaults. For risk scoring you may prefer soft-fail to a low-confidence label instead of blocking.
[25:27] Leah Ortiz: We do prefer degraded outputs rather than timeouts. How does Redwood support routing to fallback models?
[25:33] Priya Raman: Route rules in Console; you can configure fallback to a smaller quantized variant or local heuristic. There's also rate-limiter hooks so you can inject business logic.

[30:00] Daniel Park: Regarding VPC/on-prem — our security folks want private control plane and KMS integration for keys. Does dedicated support customer-managed KMS?
[30:10] Jordan Lee: Dedicated supports KMS integration and Private deployments support full customer-managed KMS/HSM. We'll attach the compliance pack (SOC2 docs) and the KMS integration guide.

[33:45] Priya Raman: For the benchmark plan — proposal: 1) Redwood runs a 7-day benchmark on a reserved Dedicated pool using your traffic trace; 2) measure p95/p99, token cost, cache-warm curves across scale events; 3) run a burst test with synthetic spikes to validate warm buffer sizing. We will need your trace and a list of hot prefixes.
[34:05] Marcus Chen: Sounds good. SLA question — if we commit to Dedicated, what guarantees on p95 SLO?
[34:12] Jordan Lee: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets for defined routes. We can map your p95 targets into route-level SLOs in the contract. Exact guarantees depend on commit size and region.

[40:02] Leah Ortiz: A nit — when replicas churn we noticed token counts jump due to cache cold starts. Any heuristics to estimate extra tokens during warm-up?
[40:15] Priya Raman: Yes, we model warm-up cost as a function of cache miss rate and average prefix length. Typical warm-up overhead is 10–30% additional tokens for the first 5–15 minutes per replica unless you pre-warm. We'll include an estimated curve in the runbook for your observed prefix distribution.

[45:20] Daniel Park: For peering and firewalling — how do you handle egress IPs and CIDR ranges?
[45:27] Jordan Lee: We provide static egress IP ranges for Dedicated control plane and instructions for VPC peering. For Private, you control network egress fully. We'll share an IP list and a network checklist.

[50:00] Marcus Chen: Ok great, recap and next steps?
[50:05] Jordan Lee: Recap: Redwood to share autoscale runbook, Warm-buffer sizing guide, quantization recommendations, and the benchmark plan. Atlas to provide 14-days traffic traces, hot-prefix list, and firewall/VPC constraints. Schedule follow-up on 2026-03-30 for benchmark kickoff.
[50:20] Samir Patel: I'll drop the links and the runbook in the CRM and Slack channel after this.
[50:28] Leah Ortiz: One last - can you also include example HPA/YAML and queueing configs?
[50:33] Priya Raman: Yes we'll attach sample YAML and a sample queueing policy.
[51:00] Marcus Chen: Thanks, appreciate it.
[51:05] Jordan Lee: Thanks team, we'll follow up.
